csci-102.title: Introduction to Programming
csci-102.topic: for and while loops in C++

recap.say: Welcome back. Last time we wrote if statements, so our programs could make decisions. Today we make them repeat work, with loops.

slide.title: Recap: making decisions
bullets: if and else pick one path

open.say: Alright, let's get started. Today is loops. A loop runs the same block of code again and again, so you don't have to copy and paste it.

slide.title: Loops
bullets: for: you know how many times

warmup.say: Quick warm-up. If I want to print the numbers one through five, how many lines would that take without a loop? Think for a second.
warmup.then: Right, five lines. Now imagine one through a thousand. That's why we need loops.

define.say: A for loop has three parts in its header: where the counter starts, the condition to keep going, and how the counter changes. The body runs once for every pass.

studentqFull.ask: What happens if the condition is never false?
studentqFull.say: Great question. The question was, what if the condition never becomes false? Then the loop runs forever. That's an infinite loop, and you have to stop the program yourself. Always check that your update moves the counter toward the end.

studentqBrief.ask: Do we have to call it i?
studentqBrief.say: No, any name works. i is just a habit. Moving on.

pair.say: Turn to your neighbor. Write a loop that adds up the numbers from one to ten. Don't run it, just trace it on paper. You have about twenty seconds.

slide.title: Think, pair, share
bullets: Sum 1 to 10 with a for loop

pairDebrief.say: Okay, bring it back. Most of you started the sum at zero and added i each time. That works, and the answer is fifty-five. A few of you set the sum to zero inside the loop, which resets it every pass, so watch for that.

concept.say: While loops are the other kind. You use one when you don't know ahead of time how many passes you need, like reading input until someone types quit.

slide.title: while loops
bullets: The check happens before each pass

question.say: So which loop would you use to read numbers until someone enters a negative one?

slide.title: Question
bullets: Read numbers until a negative appears

question.then: A while loop, because you don't know how many numbers are coming.

workedBoard1.say: Let's trace one together on the board. We'll count down from three. I start i at three, check that it's at least one, print it, then subtract one.
workedBoard1.board: i=3 prints 3, i=2 prints 2, i=1 prints 1

workedBoard2.say: After printing one, i becomes zero. Zero is not at least one, so the condition is false and the loop stops. Three passes, three lines of output.

workedDoc.say: Let's trace one under the document camera. Count down from three. I write i, check the condition, print, and update, one row at a time. When i hits zero, the check fails and we stop.

poll.say: Poll time. How many times does this loop run, if i starts at zero and keeps going while i is less than five?

poll.q: for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) runs how many times?

poll.then: Five times: zero, one, two, three and four. Starting at zero is where most off-by-one errors come from.

closeExit.say: Big idea for today. Use a for loop when you know the count, and a while loop when you don't. Before you leave, answer the exit ticket on your phone.

closeLogistics.say: Lab three on loops is due Friday at midnight. Start early, because the autograder gets slow on Thursday night. That's it for today.

recap.say: Welcome back. Last time we used structs to group related data. Today we turn that idea into classes, which bundle data with the functions that work on it.

open.say: Okay, let's get started. Today is classes. A class is a blueprint, and each object you make from it is one instance with its own data.

warmup.say: Warm-up question. If a class is a blueprint, what's something in a video game you'd model as a class? Take a second, then raise your hand.

slide.title: Warm-up
bullets: Name something in a game you'd model as a class

warmup.then: I heard player, enemy and inventory. All good. Each one has data, and things it can do.

define.say: A class keeps its data private and its functions public. Private means only the class's own code can change the data, which protects it from being changed by accident.

slide.title: public and private
bullets: public: what other code can use

studentqFull.ask: Why not just make everything public?
studentqFull.say: Good question. The question was, why not make everything public? Because then any code anywhere could set a balance to a negative number. Keeping data private means every change goes through a function that can check it.

studentqBrief.ask: Is a struct the same thing as a class?
studentqBrief.say: Almost. In C++ the only difference is the default access. We'll use classes. Moving on.

pair.say: Turn to your neighbor. Design a class for a USC course. What data does it hold, and what functions should it have? You have about twenty seconds.

pairDebrief.say: Okay, let's hear it. Most of you had a course code, a title and a list of students. For functions, add a student and drop a student. That's a solid design.
pairDebrief.board: Course: code, title, students; addStudent(), dropStudent()

concept.say: Now constructors. A constructor runs automatically when an object is created, and its job is to put the object in a valid starting state.

slide.title: Constructors
bullets: Runs when the object is created

concept.board: constructor: start in a valid state

question.say: So what's the return type of a constructor?
question.then: It has no return type at all, not even void.

workedBoard1.say: Let's write one on the board. A Point class with an x and a y. The constructor takes two numbers and stores them.

workedBoard2.say: Now when I create a point at three, four, the constructor runs, so its x is three and its y is four. Every point starts out valid.

workedDoc.say: Let me write it out under the document camera. A Point class with two private ints, and a constructor that takes two numbers. Then I create a point at three, four and check its values.

poll.say: Poll. When does a constructor run?

options: When you call it by name

poll.then: When the object is created. You never call it directly.

closeExit.say: Big idea for today. A class bundles data with the functions that protect it, and the constructor makes every object start out valid. Answer the exit ticket before you go.

closeLogistics.say: Programming assignment two is posted. It's a BankAccount class, due next Thursday. That's it for today.

recap.say: Welcome back. Last time we measured arrays with Big O. Inserting at the front of an array is slow, because everything has to shift. Today we fix that with linked lists.

slide.title: Recap: arrays
bullets: Today: a structure that fixes that

open.say: Okay, let's get started. Today is linked lists. Instead of one block of memory, each element lives in its own node, and every node points to the next one.

slide.title: Linked lists
bullets: Each node: a value and a next pointer
head points to the first node
The last node points to nullptr

warmup.say: Warm-up. In an array of a million items, how many items move when you insert at the front? Think about it, then raise your hand.

slide.title: Warm-up
bullets: Insert at the front: how many move?

warmup.then: All million of them. That's order n. Keep that in mind.

define.say: A node holds a value and a pointer to the next node, and the list only keeps track of the head. To insert at the front, make a new node, point it at the old head, and move head to it.

studentqFull.ask: So why would anyone still use arrays?
studentqFull.say: Great question. The question was, why still use arrays? Because getting the item at index five hundred is instant in an array, but in a linked list you walk five hundred nodes to get there. Every structure trades something.

studentqBrief.say: Yes, this whole unit is. Moving on.

pair.say: Turn to your neighbor. On paper, draw what happens to the pointers when you delete the second node in a list. About twenty seconds.

pairDebrief.say: Okay, let's hear it. The first node's next pointer skips over the second node and points to the third. Then you delete the second node, so you don't leak memory.

concept.say: Now, walking the list. To find a value, start at head and follow the next pointers until you find it or reach null. That's order n in the worst case.

question.say: So what's the Big O of getting the last element, if you only have a head pointer?

slide.title: Question
bullets: Cost of reaching the last node?

question.then: Order n. You have to walk the whole list, which is why some lists also keep a tail pointer.

workedBoard1.say: Let's insert at the front on the board. The list is seven, then nine. We want to add three at the front, so first I make a new node and point it at seven.

workedBoard2.say: Now head moves to the new node. The list reads three, seven, nine, and nothing else had to move.

workedDoc.say: Let me draw it under the document camera. A box for three, with an arrow to the old head at seven. Then I move head. Three steps, and no other node moved.

poll.say: Poll. What's the Big O of inserting at the front of a linked list?

poll.q: Insert at the front of a linked list?

poll.then: Order one. It's three pointer changes, no matter how long the list is.

closeExit.say: Big idea for today. Linked lists make inserting at the front cheap, and make finding something by position expensive. The exit ticket is on your phone.

closeLogistics.say: Homework three, implementing a linked list, is due next Friday. Run valgrind to check for memory leaks before you submit. That's it for today.

recap.say: Welcome back. Last time we drew supply and demand curves and found the equilibrium price. Today we ask how much buyers react when the price changes.

slide.title: Recap: equilibrium
bullets: Supply meets demand at one price

open.say: Okay, let's get started. Today is price elasticity of demand. It measures how much the quantity people buy changes when the price changes.

slide.title: Price elasticity of demand
bullets: How strongly buyers react to price
% change in quantity ÷ % change in price

warmup.say: Warm-up. If the price of gas goes up ten percent, do people buy a lot less, or about the same? Think, then raise your hand.
warmup.then: Mostly about the same, at least in the short run. People still have to drive to work. That's inelastic demand.

define.say: If quantity changes by a bigger percentage than price, demand is elastic. If it changes by a smaller percentage, demand is inelastic. We drop the minus sign and compare the number to one.

studentqFull.say: Great question. The question was, what makes demand elastic? Mostly substitutes. When there are lots of close substitutes, like one brand of cereal, people switch as soon as the price goes up.

studentqBrief.ask: Do we need to memorize the formula?
studentqBrief.say: Yes, and know how to use it. Moving on.

pair.say: Turn to your neighbor. Rank these from most to least elastic: insulin, coffee from one particular café, and movie tickets. About twenty seconds.

slide.title: Think, pair, share
bullets: insulin, one café's coffee, movie tickets

pairDebrief.say: Okay, bring it back. Most of you put the café first, because there's another café next door. Insulin is last, because people need it no matter what it costs.

concept.say: Here's why businesses care. When demand is inelastic, raising the price raises total revenue. When demand is elastic, raising the price lowers revenue, because so many buyers leave.

question.say: So if a concert sells out every single night, should the venue raise prices or lower them?
question.then: Raise them. Demand is inelastic at that price, so revenue goes up.

workedBoard1.say: Let's compute one. The price of a burrito goes from eight dollars to ten, and the number sold falls from one hundred a day to seventy.

workedBoard2.say: Thirty percent divided by twenty-five percent is one point two. That's bigger than one, so demand is elastic, and the higher price actually lowers revenue, from eight hundred dollars to seven hundred.

workedDoc.say: Let me work it under the document camera. The price goes from eight to ten, which is twenty-five percent. Quantity falls from one hundred to seventy, which is thirty percent. Thirty over twenty-five is one point two, so demand is elastic.

poll.say: Poll. The elasticity is zero point four. Is demand elastic or inelastic?
poll.then: Inelastic. It's less than one, so buyers barely react.

closeExit.say: Big idea for today. Elasticity tells you how much buyers react to price, and that decides whether raising the price helps or hurts revenue. Answer the exit ticket on your phone.

slide.title: Today's big idea
bullets: It decides what a price change does to revenue

closeLogistics.say: Problem set four on elasticity is due Tuesday. The quiz in discussion section covers chapters five and six. That's it for today.

recap.say: Welcome back. Last time we defined the derivative as a limit of slopes of secant lines. Today we find a shortcut, so you don't have to take a limit every time.

slide.title: Recap: the derivative
bullets: Today: a shortcut for powers of x

open.say: Okay, let's get started. Today is the power rule. The derivative tells you the slope of a function at a point, and for powers of x there's a quick way to find it.

warmup.say: Warm-up. What's the slope of the line y equals three x plus two? Take a second.
warmup.then: Three. A line has the same slope everywhere. Keep that in mind.

define.say: The power rule says the derivative of x to the n is n times x to the n minus one. Bring the exponent down in front, then lower the exponent by one.

studentqFull.ask: Does it work for negative exponents?
studentqFull.say: Great question. The question was, does it work for negative exponents? Yes. The derivative of x to the negative one is negative one times x to the negative two. It works for any real exponent.

studentqBrief.ask: Can we use this on the exam?
studentqBrief.say: Yes, once we prove it today. Moving on.

pair.say: Turn to your neighbor. Without the power rule, use the limit definition to find the derivative of x squared. Twenty seconds, just set it up.

slide.title: Think, pair, share
bullets: Derivative of x² from the limit definition

pairDebrief.say: Okay, bring it back. You expand x plus h squared, subtract x squared, and divide by h, which leaves two x plus h. As h goes to zero, that's two x, the same answer the power rule gives.

concept.say: The derivative of a sum is the sum of the derivatives, and constant multiples come along for the ride. So you can differentiate any polynomial one term at a time.

slide.title: Polynomials, term by term
bullets: The derivative of a constant is 0

question.say: So what's the derivative of a constant, like seven?
question.then: Zero. A constant never changes, so its slope is zero.

workedBoard1.say: Let's do one on the board. f of x equals four x cubed, minus two x, plus nine.

workedBoard2.say: One term at a time. Four x cubed becomes twelve x squared. Minus two x becomes minus two. The nine becomes zero. So f prime is twelve x squared minus two.

workedDoc.say: Let me write it out under the document camera. Four x cubed: the three comes down, so twelve x squared. Minus two x becomes minus two. The nine disappears.

poll.say: Poll. What's the derivative of x to the fifth?
poll.then: Five x to the fourth. The exponent comes down, then drops by one.

closeExit.say: Big idea for today. For powers of x, bring the exponent down and lower it by one, and take polynomials one term at a time. Answer the exit ticket on your phone.

closeLogistics.say: WebWork set five is due Thursday at eleven fifty-nine. Next time we do the product rule. That's it for today.

recap.say: Welcome back. Last time we read the op-ed on campus housing and pulled out its main claim. Today we write our own claims, and make sure they're arguable.

slide.title: Recap: finding the claim
bullets: Every argument has a main claim

open.say: Okay, let's get started. Today is the thesis. A strong thesis makes a claim a reasonable person could disagree with, and tells the reader why you believe it.

warmup.say: Warm-up. Is this a thesis: social media is popular among college students? Think about it, then raise your hand.

slide.title: Warm-up
bullets: "Social media is popular among college students."

warmup.then: Not really. It's true, but nobody would argue with it. A thesis has to be arguable.

define.say: Here's a quick test. If your sentence is a fact, a question, or so broad that nobody could disagree, it isn't a thesis yet. Add a position and a reason.

slide.title: Arguable or not?
bullets: A position plus a reason: a thesis

define.board: not a fact, not a question: a position + a reason

studentqFull.ask: Can a thesis be more than one sentence?
studentqFull.say: Great question. The question was, can a thesis be more than one sentence? Yes. In longer essays it often takes two. What matters is that both the claim and the reason are clear.

studentqBrief.ask: Does it have to go at the end of the intro?
studentqBrief.say: Usually, but it's not a rule. Moving on.

pair.say: Turn to your neighbor. Take the sentence, social media is popular among college students, and turn it into an arguable thesis. About twenty seconds.

slide.title: Think, pair, share
bullets: Revise: "Social media is popular among college students."

pairDebrief.say: Okay, let's hear a few. One pair wrote: colleges should teach media literacy, because students get most of their news from social media. That's arguable, and it gives a reason. Nice.
pairDebrief.board: Colleges should teach media literacy because...

concept.say: Every claim needs evidence. When you bring in a quote or a statistic, explain how it supports your claim. Evidence doesn't speak for itself.

question.say: So what's missing from a paragraph that drops in a quote and moves straight on?

slide.title: Question
bullets: A quote, then the next point

question.then: Analysis. You have to say how the quote supports your point.

workedBoard1.say: Let's revise one together on the board. Here's a draft: online classes are different from in-person classes.

slide.title: Revise this thesis
bullets: "Online classes are different from in-person classes."

workedBoard1.board: Draft: Online classes are different from in-person classes.

workedBoard2.say: That's a fact, not a claim. Let's take a position and add a reason. Online classes work better for review courses than for discussion seminars, because seminars depend on quick back-and-forth.
workedBoard2.board: Online works for review courses, not seminars, because...

workedDoc.say: Let me mark it up under the document camera. I'll cross out different, which doesn't say anything, and replace it with a position and a because clause.

poll.say: Poll. Which of these is an arguable thesis?

options: Should USC change its GE rules?
USC should cut GE units, because they delay graduation.

poll.then: The third one. It takes a position and gives a reason.

closeExit.say: Big idea for today. A thesis is a position plus a reason, and every piece of evidence needs your analysis. Answer the exit ticket on your phone.

slide.title: Today's big idea
bullets: Thesis: a position plus a reason

closeLogistics.say: Your thesis draft for essay two is due Monday on Brightspace. Bring a printed copy for peer review. That's it for today.

slide.title: Before next class
bullets: Bring a printed copy for peer review

recap.say: Welcome back. Last time we practiced confident line work, drawing straight lines fast instead of sketchy ones. Today we put those lines into perspective.

open.say: Okay, let's get started. Today is two-point perspective. It's how you draw a box so it looks three-dimensional, with edges that recede toward two vanishing points.

warmup.say: Warm-up. Look at a corner of this room. Do the lines along the ceiling go up or down as they move away from you? Think, then raise your hand.

slide.title: Warm-up
bullets: Ceiling lines moving away from you
Do they go up or down?

warmup.then: Down, toward your eye level. Lines above the horizon slope down to it, and lines below it slope up.

define.say: Start with a horizon line and two vanishing points. Draw the front vertical edge of the box. Then connect the top and the bottom of that edge to each vanishing point.
define.board: front edge, then lines to VP1 and VP2

studentqFull.ask: How far apart should the vanishing points be?
studentqFull.say: Great question. The question was, how far apart should the vanishing points be? Farther than you think. If they're too close, the box looks stretched and distorted, so put them near the edges of the page, or even off it.

studentqBrief.say: Not today. Freehand is the whole point of this class. Moving on.

pair.say: Turn to your neighbor. Each of you sketch a box below the horizon, then trade and check each other's vanishing lines. About twenty seconds.

slide.title: Think, pair, share
bullets: Sketch a box below the horizon
Trade and check the vanishing lines

pairDebrief.say: Okay, pencils down. The most common mistake was a back edge that wasn't vertical. In two-point perspective, every vertical edge stays straight up and down.

concept.say: Where you put the box changes what you see. Below the horizon, you see its top. Above the horizon, you see its bottom, like looking up at a building.

slide.title: Eye level changes the view
bullets: Below the horizon: you see the top
Above the horizon: you see the bottom

concept.board: below: see the top; above: see the bottom

question.say: So if a box sits exactly on the horizon line, can you see its top?

slide.title: Question
bullets: A box exactly on the horizon

question.then: No. At eye level, the top face lines up with your eye, so it disappears.

workedBoard1.say: Let's draw one on the board. The horizon goes here, the vanishing points at both edges, and the front edge of the box just below the horizon.
workedBoard1.board: front edge, then connect it to both VPs

workedBoard2.say: Now I drop the two side edges straight down, connect their corners back to the opposite vanishing points, and the top face appears. That's a box in two-point perspective.
workedBoard2.board: side edges vertical, then close the top face

workedDoc.say: Let me sketch it under the document camera so you can see the speed of the lines. Front edge, lines to both vanishing points, side edges straight down, then close the top.

poll.say: Poll. In two-point perspective, which edges stay perfectly vertical?
poll.then: All of the vertical edges. Only the horizontal edges recede to the vanishing points.

closeExit.say: Big idea for today. A horizon line, two vanishing points, and vertical edges that stay vertical. Before you go, answer the exit ticket on your phone.

closeLogistics.say: For Wednesday, fill two sketchbook pages with fifty boxes in two-point perspective, at different heights. That's it for today.

slide.title: Before next class
bullets: Vary the height above and below the horizon
